title: Feature Design

writing.exampleCaption: Each build compiles exactly one `paint`, chosen by whether `color` is on.
writing.explanation:
Cargo features are unified across a dependency graph, so disabling one consumer's feature may not disable it globally. Prefer additive capabilities and avoid features that make the same API mean incompatible things.

A feature is a named, additive capability a crate can enable at compile time. `#[cfg(feature = "color")]` includes code only when that feature is active; another branch can provide behavior without it. A feature is not a runtime switch, so a binary cannot toggle it after compilation. The public API exposed under different feature sets should be understandable and tested in each supported configuration.

Cargo unifies feature requests for the same package in a dependency graph. If one dependency path asks for feature A and another asks for feature B, the package may be built with both. That makes mutually exclusive features fragile: downstream users can accidentally activate the combination. Prefer features that add independent capabilities and keep a sensible default. If two backends truly cannot coexist, document and enforce that constraint explicitly, or consider a different design.

Create a tiny crate with a `color` feature and compile it with and without `--features color`. Then add two dependents that request different features of the same library and inspect the resulting feature graph with `cargo tree -e features`. Test `--no-default-features` if you claim that mode works. Avoid assuming that setting `default-features = false` at one edge globally disables defaults; another path can enable them. Feature design is part of the compatibility contract, not only a way to reduce compile time.

A feature name should describe the capability it adds. Avoid names that merely encode an internal implementation file, because external users will depend on the public meaning over time.
writing.feedback: Additive capabilities only add code, so the union Cargo builds still compiles. Mutually exclusive features break as soon as two dependents enable both.

writing.task: Declare both features, build with `--features backend_a,backend_b`, and read the error. Then redesign them as additive capabilities that can be on at once.

recall.question: A library offers mutually exclusive features `backend-a` and `backend-b`. Why is that design fragile?
recall.answer: Cargo unifies feature requests for one package across the dependency graph, so if two dependents ask for different backends, the library is built with both. Prefer additive features; if two options truly cannot coexist, document and enforce that explicitly.

recall.question: How does a Cargo feature such as `color` differ from a runtime configuration switch?
recall.answer: It selects code at compile time through `#[cfg(feature = "color")]`; a built binary contains only one branch and cannot toggle it later. Each supported feature combination therefore has to be built and tested separately.
